Very interesting art on the Arc de Triomphe. The first thing that really caught my eye is the sculptural group, Le Départ de 1792 (La Marseillaise) AKA The Departure of the Volunteers 1792.

This is the first of the four sculpture groups chronologically. At 12:00 we see a very angry-looking angel or some greek/roman god/goddess summoning humans to war. Scanning counterclockwise we see the trumpeteer sounding the call to battle, then a very sober looking soldier crouched and on-guard against an imminent threat. Front and center is the leader with his face showing the concern and anguish that comes with full comprehension of the carnage and death ahead. The general has the finest armor with shin-guards and decorative (yet functional) reinforced nipples. His arm is around a boy of 11 or 12 who's been supplied with a helmet and a sword yet his twig and berries are literally flapping in the wind. To the child's right we see the face of a man who has seen the true horrors of battle.

Finally comes the WOW. In the background, behind the soldier and the general, we see [[[him]]]. The right hand points the leader in the direction of war and destruction while the left hand covers the mouth indicating whispers and secrets. This face is the only one without a classic aquiline nose.
